title: Fix snow lingering when the Dock moves between displays
body:
## Problem

After moving the Dock to another display, its snow could remain on the previous display even though the Dock itself was no longer there.

The two coordinate sources could disagree during the move: the Dock window had already moved, while `SLSGetDockRectWithReason` still returned a reserved rect on the previous display. The last `DockOverlay` frame could also remain visible without being redrawn.

## Changes

- Determine the Dock's display from the center of its actual `CGWindowList` window.
- Use the SkyLight reserved rect only when it belongs to the same display.
- Fall back to calculating the Dock shelf from the display containing its window when the reserved rect is stale.
- Let the Dock's snow fall when it disappears instead of preserving it as snow on another Space.
- Hide `DockOverlay` immediately when the Dock or its snow is gone, and show it again when snow appears.

## Testing

- `./build.sh` completes successfully.
- Verified manually: snow was allowed to accumulate on the Dock, then the Dock was moved between displays. The snow and stale overlay disappeared from the previous display, and snow accumulated correctly on the Dock at its new location.

title: Add a cherry blossom mode
body:
## Summary

A fourth mode, Cherry Blossom: sakura petals fall instead of snow on the Mac, Windows and Linux. They behave like autumn leaves in the air and in heaps, but look like petals: notched, curved like a spoon, pink at the base, glowing when the light comes through them, and browning at the edges as they lie with Wilt Petals on. Now and then a whole flower spins down on its stalk.

## Changes

- Mac: the `blossom` mode, its menu items (Cherry Blossom, Wilt Petals, Petals on Windows, Clear Petals) and menu-bar icon; the petal and flower drawing in Metal.
- Core: the leaf physics carries petals (`leafy`), with `blossom()` and `wilts()`; a test that petals fall and lie as leaves do.
- Windows and Linux: the same drawing in HLSL and GLSL, the menu items, settings and tray icons.
- README and PRODUCT describe the mode, and list Deep Interaction.

## Test plan

- [x] macOS 27: petals, whole flowers, withering and the glow, by eye and in offscreen renders
- [x] Linux: GLSL validated with glslangValidator, rendered in the headless Sway bench
- [x] Windows: HLSL compiled with vkd3d, the app built with cargo-xwin

title: Lay the drift along the bottom under a full-screen app
body:
## Summary

With Show over Full Screen on, the snow kept stopping short of the taskbar or panel a full-screen app had put away, so its drift hung over an empty strip along the bottom (#59). Now the snow reaches the bottom of the display while a full-screen app is in front; the drift falls there as off a closing window, and rides up again when the taskbar or panel comes back. Fixes #59.

## Changes

- Core: `lower_ground` drops the ground's snow from where it lay, `raise_ground` brings the drift up with the ground, and both keep what is falling and the snow on windows where it is on the screen; `lift_onto` lets a returning ledge take up the drift under it.
- Windows: a display covered by a full-screen app (for 0.3 s, so the transition's steps don't rebuild it) gets an overlay over the whole display, through `sync_screens`; turning Behind Taskbar on and off moves the ground the same way.
- Linux: the layer surface's margins drop to zero under a full-screen app; a bottom panel's shelf is put away with it and takes its drift up again on return; niri's overview doesn't count.
- Linux: full-screen windows under fractional scaling, a fraction of a pixel short of the display, now count as full screen, which also fixes the snow making way for them with the setting off.

## Test plan

- [x] Windows 11: the drift falls to the bottom entering full screen and rises onto the taskbar leaving it; same for Behind Taskbar; windows' snow and falling flakes stay put
- [x] KDE Plasma (Fedora, scale 1.7): the same with the panel's shelf
- [x] `cargo test` in `core/` (new tests for the ground dropping and rising, and the panel taking up the drift)

title: Add Deep Interaction: snow on a selection dragged across the desktop
body:
## Summary

Deep Interaction, a new menu setting on Windows and the Mac, off by default: the snow also settles on the rubber band a drag across the desktop's empty space draws to select icons, and drops off it when the button comes up. The band has no window of its own, so it is followed from the mouse.

## Changes

- Windows: the primary button (`GetAsyncKeyState`, swapped buttons respected) going down on the desktop's icon view starts a band from there to the pointer; a `SysDragImage` window means an icon is being dragged instead. Any band wider than a ledge's eight columns holds snow, however thin.
- Mac: a global mouse-down monitor (no permission needed for the mouse) checks that Finder's desktop or the wallpaper is the first thing drawn at the press, past the window server's clear strips; a window at the dragging level means an icon drag.
- The band is a surface behind every window that hides nothing; turning the setting off drops it.
- The setting sits under Snow on Windows and needs it; README mentions it. Linux has none: Wayland compositors give no way to see the mouse's buttons.

## Test plan

- [x] Windows 11: a band dragged across the desktop catches snow, thin ones too; it falls when the button comes up; dragging an icon catches none
- [x] macOS 27: the same on Finder's desktop
- [x] With the setting off, no band catches snow

title: Let the snow cling to rounded corners
body:
## Summary

The snow stopped about halfway round a rounded corner, its end hanging over the curve: the slump measured repose on the snow's surface, so any layer on a steepening bed slid off. Now a layer clings to its bed as long as the bed is no steeper than about 55 degrees. Desktop widgets on macOS 27 also get their real corner, so the snow follows it instead of lifting off.

## Changes

- `CLING_SLOPE` (1.4, about 55°): the slump allows the bed's own fall, up to that slope, on top of the angle of repose, in `SnowLayer.relax` and the core's `relax` alike.
- Widgets' corner on macOS 27 is 31 points (22 before), measured from the widget's outer edge against the snow's superellipse; their frame, inset 8 points from the window, matches their accessibility frame.

## Test plan

- [x] macOS 27: the snow wraps about two thirds round the corners of widgets, windows and the Dock and thins out, flush with the edge (checked in ⌘⇧4 screenshots, pixel by pixel)
- [x] `cargo test` in `core/`

title: Shape the snow to each window's own corners
body:
## Summary

macOS 27 rounds every window's corners alike, at 16 points, tighter than the 18 the snow assumed, so on the corners it lay off the window's curve. The radius is now taken from the window server for each window. Fixes #76.

## Changes

- `Corners` asks the window server for windows' corner radii (`SLSWindowQueryWindows` and `SLSWindowIteratorGetResolvedCornerRadii`), once for each window that shows up.
- A window reported without rounding, and systems without these calls, take 16 points from macOS 27 and 18 before.

## Test plan

- [x] macOS 27.0.1: the window server reports 16 points for Finder, Chrome, System Settings and others; the snow follows their corners
- [x] A window drawing its own frame (Rio) reports 0 and takes 16

title: Use macOS 27's uniform app-window corner radius
body:
## Description

Apple says that macOS 27 gives every window the same tighter corner radius, including windows from third-party apps that have not been updated.

 From the official WWDC26 Keynote, at 8:48:

> And every window on macOS now has the same tighter corner radius ensuring greater consistency across all of your apps, even if they haven’t been updated.

Snowhush currently uses an 18 pt radius for ordinary application windows. On macOS 27 this may place snow on a different curve from the visible window frame.

Apple's statement does not specify the numerical radius. A possible value to verify is 16 pt, but this should be checked against the released version of macOS 27 before changing the model.

## Questions
- What is the exact outer window radius in the released version of macOS 27?
- Should Snowhush use that value on macOS 27 while retaining 18 pt on older versions?

title: Let window screenshots pick the window under the snow
body:
## Summary

With Snowhush running, the screenshot tool's window picker (⌘⇧4 then Space, or ⌘⇧5's Capture Selected Window) picked the snow's overlay instead of the window under it: it captured the snow alone, or, with Show in Screenshots off, failed with "Unable to capture window image". The picker goes by what is drawn under the pointer, and the Metal-drawn overlay counts as drawn everywhere; it settles on its window as Space is pressed. Fixes #65.

## Changes

- `ScreenshotWatch` follows SystemUIServer with a process source and catches the moment it starts `screencapture` for a screenshot shortcut, at no cost otherwise.
- When that `screencapture` picks (`-i` for ⌘⇧4, `-U` for ⌘⇧5), the overlays order out until it exits; ⌘⇧3 is left alone.
- With Show in Screenshots on, the overlays come back as soon as a region is dragged out, so region screenshots still take the snow in.

title: Keep snow on the Spotlight bar while typing
body:
## Summary

On every keystroke Spotlight's window (owned by Siri, layer 23) flips between its bar and a transparent window the size of the screen. title: fix: keep snow stable in Show Desktop and Spotlight
body:
## What I ran into

I use Snowhush 0.7.1 on macOS 27.2 with two displays: an external display above the MacBook's built-in one. Behind Windows is enabled.

I noticed two problems:

1. Clicking the wallpaper activates macOS's native Show Desktop feature. Application windows move away as expected, but snow also disappears from the desktop widgets and the Dock, even though they remain visible. The drift at the bottom of the screen stays.
2. While typing in Spotlight, snow on windows and desktop widgets flickers or gets clipped on every keystroke. Again, the drift at the bottom remains visible.

While investigating the first case, I also noticed that a terminal window from the external display could cross the built-in display's coordinates during Show Desktop without being visible there. Snow on the widgets was clipped by this invisible window.

## Root causes

- The tracker treated every screen-sized `WindowManager` window as Mission Control or App Exposé. Show Desktop uses a level-18 shield, whereas Mission Control and App Exposé use level 19. The false positive emptied the whole window-surface list.
- Spotlight is backed by a `Siri` window that alternates between a compact panel and a transparent `1512×870` window below the menu bar. The latter covers less than 90% of the whole screen, so the previous check did not recognize it as a transparent full-screen overlay and added it as an occluder for all other surfaces.
- With separate Spaces on each display, a window can intersect another display's bounds without being shown there. Its frame was nevertheless used as an occluder.

## Changes

- Recognize Mission Control and App Exposé shields only at the expected window level.
- Use the existing `fillsScreen` check, which accounts for the menu bar, for transparent overlays such as Siri and Notification Center.
- Ignore ordinary windows that belong to another display's current Space instead of letting them hide snow on this display.

## Testing

Tested on macOS 27.2 with built-in and external displays, with Behind Windows enabled:

- `./build.sh`
- Show Desktop preserves snow on the Dock and desktop widgets without flickering.
- Typing in Spotlight no longer clips or flickers snow on other surfaces.
- An invisible window from the other display no longer hides widget snow.
- Mission Control and App Exposé still keep snow off thumbnails and restore it afterward.

## Out of scope

Snow still returns after Mission Control and App Exposé with the existing 0.2–0.5 second delay, which follows the system animation. This PR does not change that behavior.

Related to #37, which implements broader display/Space ownership and snow handoff between displays. This change only prevents windows from another display's Space from becoming occluders; it does not implement snow handoff.

title: Add rain as a third mode
body:
## Summary
Rain comes back as a third entry in the Mode menu, on Mac, Windows and Linux. It beats down and splashes where it lands, and on the tops of windows, desktop widgets, the Dock and the taskbar it spatters the glass and sets drops running down it like water on a window, or hanging under bottom edges until they let go. A Performance menu adds a Max option that draws every frame at the display's full rate.

## Changes
- Core: `Mode` enum (`set_mode`, `switch_mode`) replaces the autumn flag; `simulation/rain.rs` with streak rain, splashes, running, hanging and smeared drops, spray and film on the glass
- Running drops come from 7% of hits on top edges, catch on specks, gather the spray they meet, lurch on and leave a wet film and a trail of uneven beads
- Drops hang under bottom edges, follow rounded corners, and let go once heavy; a drop that falls off one window runs on down the one below
- The cursor knocks hanging drops off and smears running ones into lines of beads; dragging a window sideways trails its drops, shaking it throws them off
- Mac desktop widgets now catch snow and rain; rain also runs down the Dock, the Windows taskbar and a Plasma panel in front of it
- Drops on the glass drawn as liquid glass (Metal, HLSL and GLSL alike), with uneven outlines that answer to how they run
- Rain doesn't pile up, so Accumulate, Melt Snow and Clear Snow step aside and Snow on Windows becomes Rain on Windows
- Performance menu (Default, Max) on all platforms
- README and PRODUCT.md describe Rain, Halloween and the newer menu items

## Test plan
- [x] `cargo fmt --check` for core, windows and linux
- [x] `cargo test --locked` in core
- [x] Mac build; Windows and Linux builds
- [x] Mac: rain on windows, widgets and the Dock; hanging drops, smearing, shaking, dragging
- [x] Windows: rain and the wet glass on real hardware, taskbar ledge

title: snow issue
fix: stop Behind Windows overlays flickering every second
body:
## Summary

With Behind Windows on, the snow (or leaves) could blink about once a second. It showed up most clearly with more than one display: sometimes one monitor, sometimes another, sometimes not at all for a while.

The once-a-second chores pass was calling `raise` on every overlay every time. Behind Windows those overlays are child windows of the same desktop `Progman`. Each call tries to tuck that overlay just under the desktop icons. With several monitors, only one of them can sit in that slot, so they keep shoving each other. The desktop layer recomposites, and the snow flickers. Overlays above windows are separate topmost windows, so the same call does not do this there — the bug is Behind Windows only.

`raise` itself still matters: it keeps the snow under the icons and above live wallpapers that land in the same layer later. This PR does not remove that. It only stops doing it on a fixed one-second timer when nothing in the layer has changed.

## What changed

- Behind Windows: raise when the desktop layer's child list changes (Explorer rebuild, a live wallpaper appearing, and the like), not on every chores tick.
- When raise does run, skip `SetWindowPos` if the overlay is already under the icons with only other Snowhush overlays between it and them.

Above-windows behaviour is unchanged: raise still runs from the chores pass as before.

## How to reproduce

1. Windows 11, ideally two or three monitors (easier to see; one monitor can still show it).
2. Turn on Behind Windows.
3. Leave the snow running on the desktop, windows moved aside or Win+D so the drift is visible.
4. Watch for about half a minute without touching the overlays.

Without the fix, the drift blinks roughly once a second, often on one display then another. With the fix, it should stay steady.

## Testing

Windows 11, three displays, Behind Windows on: watched the desktop drift for several minutes with no flicker. Toggled Behind Windows off and on; overlays still sit under the icons afterward.

title: feat: let notification toasts sweep the snow on Windows
body:
Part of #31: the Windows side, as @hafn-g outlined in #58.

## Summary

Notification toasts now take part in the snow:

- A toast sliding in (or arriving in place) sweeps the snow (or leaves) off the drift under it and pushes it ahead, with the falling snow along.
- It does not grow a ledge of its own: toasts stay `COVER_ONLY`, so snow is scraped aside rather than settling on the banner text.
- The slide-in is modelled when Windows parks the toast at its final rect while the content animates, same idea as KDE in #34.
- As agreed in #31, it follows Snow on Windows and has no menu option of its own. The shared piece is a `sweep` in `core/`; Linux only gained the new `WindowSurface` fields so it still builds.

## How it works

Toast banners are `Windows.UI.Core.CoreWindow` windows from `ShellExperienceHost` (sometimes `ShellHost`). `EnumWindows` often misses them, so the tracker also keeps ones noticed through WinEvents and merges them into the list. Size filters keep other CoreWindows out.

The toast rect is usually already final on arrival, so the left-edge motion is modelled (exponential ease, matching the system slide when client-area animation is on). While that edge moves, `sweep_toasts` scrapes the band down to the ground and throws the snow ahead; app window ledges are not rewritten every frame.

## Notes

- Geometry was checked on Windows 11 (build 28000) with bottom-right toasts. Other builds may size the CoreWindow a little differently around the card.
- Tall toasts: the sweep band is capped; the scrape still clears the drift the banner sits in.
- Multiple displays: each overlay follows toasts on its own monitor.
- Dismiss / swap: when the toast goes, the sweep edge is dropped; no snow was held on the banner, so nothing extra falls off it.
- Behind Windows is unchanged; this PR only adds the sweep path.

## Testing

On Windows 11 (three displays), checked with real toasts and a local test notifier:

- [x] A single toast: sweep of the drift, falling snow pushed aside
- [x] Leaves mode
- [x] Toast with Snow on Windows on
- [x] Toast with Behind Windows on
- [x] Reduce / no client-area animation (one-shot scrape)
- [x] Second and third displays
- [x] No snow settling on the toast text
- [x] Rain mode (after rebasing onto v0.7.0)

title: feat: let notification banners sweep the snow on macOS
body:
Part of #31: the macOS side. The Windows side comes in a separate PR from @gubinme.

## Summary

Notification banners now take part in the snow:

- A banner sliding in sweeps the snow (or leaves, or petals) off the windows under it and pushes it ahead, with the falling snow along.
- While it shows, snow settles on its top edge like on a window, never over its text.
- When it slides away, it carries its snow with momentum; the screen's right edge scrapes it off like a wall, whether or not another display is there, since the banner doesn't move on to it.
- Closed with its ✕ button, it shrinks in place and drops its snow straight down; with Reduce Motion on, banners fade in place, so they sweep nothing and drop their snow straight down too.
- Swaps (a new notification replacing the one showing), hovering (which keeps a banner up), and alert-style notifications (which stay until dismissed) are handled.
- While Notification Center's window is up, the overlay drops just below its level, so banners and the opened Notification Center panel stay in front of the snow. The pointer over them no longer moves the snow hidden behind.

## How it works

The window list has no window for a banner, only Notification Center's clear screen-sized window, so the banner's place and motion come from the fixed way macOS lays banners out and animates them, measured on macOS 26. When they move comes from Notification Center's processor time (`proc_pid_rusage`), and swaps from usernoted's. No Accessibility permission and no AX polling.

With no notification showing, the cost is two `proc_pid_rusage` calls a frame, about 1 µs. The window list is read only while Notification Center is busy or its window is up.

As agreed in #31, it follows Snow on Windows and has no menu option of its own. The banner logic is in a new `NotificationBanner.swift`; the simulation only gained a `sweep` for a surface sliding in.

## Notes

- Banner geometry and timing (344 pt wide, 16 pt margins, slide easing, 4.97 s lifetime, 416 pt panel) were measured on macOS 26 only. macOS 14, 15 and 27 are untested: banners there may sit or move a little differently. Notification Center's process is found by its bundle ID, and its window is looked up again whenever Notification Center gets busy, so a window that comes and goes with the banners, as it may on other versions, is still picked up in time.
- Tall banners: the snow lies on a standard banner's top edge, which longer banners share, so it still sits right.
- Multiple displays: banners show on the main display, and only that display's snow reacts. Making an external display the main one is untested.
- Swiping a banner away isn't detected separately; its snow drops in place as Notification Center's window goes.

## Testing

On macOS 26 (MacBook Air, plus an LG UltraWide as a second display), checked on screen recordings:

- [x] A single banner: sweep, snow on its top edge, slide-out with momentum
- [x] Two notifications in a row (swap)
- [x] Hover for a moment and for several seconds, then leave
- [x] Close with ✕
- [x] Long, multi-line banner
- [x] Notification Center opened over a banner, and a banner arriving with it open; the pointer over the panel leaves the snow behind alone, while the Dock's snow under it still reacts
- [x] Click on the banner's text (opens the app)
- [x] Alert style: stays put with its snow, ignores Notification Center's background work, closes cleanly
- [x] Reduce Motion
- [x] Do Not Disturb (delivered, no banner: nothing happens)
- [x] An app in full screen
- [x] Second display, with either display active
- [x] Leaves mode
- [x] Rain mode
- [x] Cherry blossom mode (after rebasing onto v0.8.0)

title: Move Halloween into the Mode menu for any day
body:
## Summary
Halloween was a seasonal item that only showed from October 30 to dawn on November 1. It now sits in the Mode menu under Snow and Autumn Leaves, after a separator, on every platform and all year. It still comes on by itself in season, and only shows over snow.

## Changes
- Core: `halloween::Today` and `halloween::Choice` decide whether Halloween is wanted: turned on from the menu, or in season and not turned off for that year
- Turned on in season, Halloween ends with the season; turned on any other day, it stays on until turned off
- Halloween is greyed out under Autumn Leaves and comes back on returning to Snow
- New settings keys (`halloweenOn`, `halloweenSkipped`), so last season's stored choice does not turn Halloween on all year
- No ghost rises while the mode is switching, so none is made of leaves
- Mac, Windows (glass and native menu) and Linux tray menus updated alike

## Test plan
- [x] Core tests, including the season and toggle rules
- [x] Mac: Halloween under the Mode separator, on and off, greyed under Autumn Leaves
- [x] Windows: same in the glass tray menu
- [x] Linux: same in the tray menu

title: Add Show over Full Screen on all platforms
body:
## Summary

A new menu setting, Show over Full Screen, keeps the snow over full-screen apps and games instead of fading it out of their way, as asked in #52 for borderless full-screen games. It sits under Behind Windows, is off by default, and is greyed out while Behind Windows is on, since the snow is under the app then anyway.

Closes #52

## Changes

- Mac (`ScreenSnow.swift`, `AppDelegate.swift`, `Preferences.swift`): with `overFullScreen`, no full-screen Space counts as covering the display, and turning it on or off fades the snow in or out on the spot.
- Windows (`snow.rs`, `app.rs`, `prefs.rs`): skips the check for a window filling the display.
- Linux (`snow.rs`, `screen.rs`, `tray.rs`, `prefs.rs`): skips the check, and puts the overlay on the `overlay` layer rather than `top`, since compositors draw full-screen windows over `top`.
- Saved as `showOverFullScreen` on every platform.

## Test plan

- [x] Mac: the snow shows over a full-screen app with the setting on; turned off there, it fades out
- [x] Windows: the snow shows over a full-screen window with the setting on
- [x] Linux (KDE): the snow shows over a full-screen window with the setting on
- [x] The item is greyed out with Behind Windows on
- [x] `cargo fmt --check` for core, windows and linux; clippy shows no new warnings

title: Draw the Windows tray menu on blurred glass
body:
## Summary

On Windows 11 22H2 and later, the tray menu is now a panel of blurred, tinted glass with submenus opening beside it, in place of the system's popup menu. This builds on #43 by J-n-n-k, whose commit is kept here: the list of entries, the menu's loop and the fallback to the system's menu come from it, while the drawing and placement are reworked.

## Changes

- `windows/src/menu.rs`:
  - Panels drawn with Direct2D over a blur of what is behind them, through the accent policy (the undocumented `SetWindowCompositionAttribute` the taskbar uses), tinted for the taskbar's light or dark theme. The system's Acrylic backdrop (`DWMSBT_TRANSIENTWINDOW`) takes over when transparency effects are off or the accent policy fails.
  - DWM rounds the corners and casts the shadow. Labels use Segoe UI Variable, and the marks and chevrons use Segoe Fluent Icons.
  - The menu is placed with `CalculatePopupWindowPosition`, as a system menu is.
  - Submenus open beside their panel after the system's menu delay, or at once on a click.
  - Keyboard: arrows, Enter, Space and Esc.
- `windows/src/app.rs`: `entries` describes the menu once, with Intensity and Mode as radio groups. The system's menu is built from it on Windows 10 and Windows 11 before 22H2, with a screen reader or high contrast on, or if the panel can't be shown.
- `windows/src/screen.rs`: the snow stays under the menu, as it does under the system's popups.
- `windows/src/tracker.rs`: `windows_build` is shared with the menu.
- `windows/Cargo.toml`: `Win32_UI_Controls`, for `MARGINS`.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo xwin clippy` shows no new warnings
- [x] Windows 11 with a dark taskbar: the wallpaper shows through the blur, and the submenus open beside the menu (to its left at the screen's right edge)
- [ ] Light theme
- [ ] Transparency effects off
- [ ] Keyboard, and a click outside closes the menu
- [ ] Windows 10 falls back to the system's menu
- [ ] Several monitors and display scales

title: Stamp the Mac app with the SDK it is built with
body:
## Summary

Swift Build, which `swift build` now uses by default, records the deployment target (14.0) as the binary's SDK version. macOS 26 and later then run Snowhush in its compatibility look, so the menu bar menu had no Liquid Glass. `build.sh` now stamps the binary with the SDK it was really built with.

## Changes

- `build.sh`: copies the binary into the bundle with `vtool -set-build-version macos <LSMinimumSystemVersion> <SDK version> -replace`, before signing.

## Test plan

- [x] `vtool -show-build`: the arm64 and x86_64 slices show `minos 14.0`, `sdk 27.2` (before: `sdk 14.0`)
- [x] macOS 27: the menu, the Mode submenu and the Intensity slider are drawn with Liquid Glass
- [ ] The next release signs and notarizes as before

title: Keep snow off Mission Control's thumbnails
body:
## Summary
In Mission Control snow settled on the shrunk windows and on the Spaces bar for a while, then vanished. The window tracker told Mission Control apart only by its screen-sized shield, which drops out as Mission Control opens over a full-screen app and between Spaces; in those gaps its windows looked like ordinary ones.

## Changes
- Mission Control is also recognised by its bar of Spaces along the top (WindowManager, above the normal layer, the screen's width, short), which stays the whole time it shows; one check serves the tracker and the full-screen handling.
- No WindowManager window above the normal layer (shield, bar, thumbnails, labels) carries snow.

## Test plan
- [x] Mission Control opened over a full-screen film: no snow on the shrunk windows or the Spaces bar
- [x] Mission Control from a desktop, moving between Spaces inside it
- [x] Back on the desktop, snow settles on windows as before

title: Keep the snow out of full-screen apps' way
body:
## Summary
Since v0.5.7 (#22) the Mac overlays sit in a Space of their own that shows over every other one, so snow fell over full-screen apps, films included. The snow now fades out of a full-screen app's way and rests until the app goes, following the transitions macOS animates. On Windows and Linux, where the snow already hid over full-screen apps at once, it now fades out and back in.

## Changes
- Mac: a display covered by a full-screen app's Space fades its overlays out, then pauses drawing; the snow keeps falling while it fades and comes back where it stopped.
- Going full screen (the green button, a video's full-screen key), the new full-screen Space is spotted as it is added, before the window server hides the overlays for the move, so they never flash back.
- Swiping between a desktop and a full-screen app, the snow follows the slide both ways: as much shows as the square of the desktop's share of the screen, read from the window list (the app's windows and the desktop's, against their frames on their own Spaces). Turning a swipe back brings it back with it; passing through an empty desktop keeps it.
- Under a full-screen app nothing is drawn; a 4 Hz lookout reads the window list for the desktop coming back. With Snow on Windows off, the window list is read only while a full-screen app is there to swipe to.
- Mission Control showing over a full-screen app's Space (its shield or its bar of Spaces) keeps the snow until the app fills the screen.
- Windows: the DirectComposition visual gets an effect group whose opacity fades the snow out over 0.25 s and in over 0.35 s; the overlay hides once it is gone.
- Linux: a last pass multiplies the frame by the opacity (blend `ZERO, CONSTANT_ALPHA`), the same fade; the surface is cleared once it is gone.

## Test plan
- [x] Mac: video full screen with its key and the green button, no flash
- [x] Mac: swipes to and from a full-screen app, slow, quick, turned back, through an empty desktop, with Snow on Windows on and off
- [x] Mac: Mission Control picking the film, moving between Spaces inside it, opened from the film
- [x] Windows: full screen in and out, Alt-Tab, the snow fades
- [x] Linux: full screen in and out, the snow fades back in (also in the headless Sway bench)

title: Switch the license to PolyForm Noncommercial
body:
## Summary
Paid apps built on Snowhush's code have started to appear, and MIT allows that. From the next release Snowhush is under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0: anyone can still use, share, fork and change it for free, keeping the copyright notice, but selling it or anything built on its code isn't allowed. Versions up to 0.6.1 stay under MIT.

## Changes
- `LICENSE`: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, verbatim from the PolyForm project, with a `Required Notice:` line naming the author and the repository.
- README: the License section says what is and isn't allowed and that versions up to 0.6.1 were MIT; "free and open source" becomes "free, source available", since a noncommercial license isn't open source by the OSI definition.
- Packaging: the RPM spec, both PKGBUILDs and the AUR `.SRCINFO` use the SPDX identifier `PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0`.

## Test plan
- [ ] CI: the Linux packages still build with the new license field
- [ ] GitHub shows the new license on the repository page

title: Stop unwithered leaves from heaping up without limit
body:
## Summary
With Wither Leaves off, the leaf heap along the bottom of the screen grew without limit and buried the whole screen within an hour or two (reported on TikTok). Snow tops out at its layer's capacity because each flake adds less as a drift fills; falling leaves added their full bulk however deep the heap was. Melt Snow and Wither Leaves share one setting, so anyone who turned melting off for snow got this in autumn.

## Changes
- A falling leaf adds its bulk to a heap only while the heap is below the layer's capacity (about 40 pt on the ground, 14 pt on windows); above it the leaf still lies on top and fades as usual. Same change in the Mac simulation and in core.
- A hard stop rather than snow's gradual fill, so heaps with withering on stay exactly as in v0.6.0.
- Test `unwithered_leaves_heap_no_deeper_than_snow`: Heavy leaves for 15 minutes without withering stay under 60 pt (166 pt before the fix).

## Test plan
- [x] Core tests pass
- [x] Mac release build
- [x] Simulated 2 h per intensity at 1512×982 without withering: the ground heap peaks at 45–51 pt (was 866 pt on Steady and thousands on Heavy); snow without melting peaks at 46 pt
- [x] With withering on, heaps unchanged: 16–23 pt peak, 6–10 pt mean
- [ ] Mac: Wither Leaves off for an hour, heap stops growing

title: Add an autumn leaves mode
body:
## Summary

Adds an Autumn Leaves mode on macOS, Windows and Linux: leaves fall instead of snow, turn and swing on the way down, settle in heaps that show the leaves they are made of, scatter under the cursor and come off windows that are shaken, dragged or resized. Also fixes the Space swipe wind on the Mac, the spill cone in #42 and Behind Windows with Accumulate, and gives the tray icons the system's look.

## Changes

- Menu: Snowfall is now Intensity; a Mode submenu picks Snow or Autumn Leaves; Melt Snow, Snow on Windows and Clear Snow become Wither Leaves, Leaves on Windows and Clear Leaves; Open at Login sits with Check for Updates and Quit.
- Leaves: their own fall, sway and spin, motion blur over a short exposure, heaps drawn as leaves, lying leaves on top that fly off under the cursor and in the swipe's wind.
- Heap physics: lift and slide by the window's motion with leaf friction, a shake throws the whole heap as leaves, resizing from either edge sheds leaves instead of dragging them, closed windows drop their leaves.
- Mac: the three-finger swipe between Spaces is detected past full-size windows, so its wind blows the snow again.
- Windows and Linux: the tray icon is a monochrome glyph following the light or dark taskbar and KDE Plasma panel.
- Fixes #42: snow pouring off a window no longer heaps up above the point it pours from.
- Behind Windows with Accumulate: snow still settles on the windows.
- README describes the mode.

## Test plan

- [x] `cd core && cargo test`
- [x] `cargo fmt --check` in core, windows and linux
- [x] Mac: leaves, heaps, cursor, shake, resize, swipe wind
- [x] Windows 11: leaves, heap release on shake and resize, tray icon
- [x] Linux KDE Plasma 6: leaves, heaps
- [ ] Linux KDE Plasma 6: tray icon white on a dark panel
- [ ] CI builds for all three platforms
